definition.text: The national-accounts term for the depreciation of fixed assets: the fall in their current value over a period through wear, normal obsolescence and normal accidental damage.

facts.text: It is valued at current market prices rather than historic cost, which is why the System of National Accounts avoids the word depreciation.
The UN manual says it may account for 10 per cent or more of total GDP.
Net measures such as net domestic product and net national income are found by deducting it from GDP and GNI.
Net national income shows the income actually available for consumption and new investment, making it a better measure of economic welfare than GDP.
It excludes the depletion or degradation of non-produced assets such as land, mineral deposits, coal, oil and natural gas.
It also excludes assets destroyed by war or rare major natural disasters.
Critics note that its 'economic' valuation yields figures that differ from standard accounting practice.

title: Capital consumption allowance
article: Consumption of fixed capital#Capital Consumption Allowance

definition.text: The part of GDP due to depreciation, measuring what a country must spend just to maintain, rather than grow, its productive capacity.

facts.text: It covers wear and tear on physical capital plus the investment needed to maintain human capital, such as educating workers to replace retirees.
GDP equals net domestic product plus the capital consumption allowance.

definition.text: In accounting, the fall in an asset's value as it is used and wears out, and the spreading of its original cost over the years it is useful.

facts.text: Businesses depreciate long-term assets for both accounting and tax purposes.
Depreciation reduces reported net income but does not require a current outlay of cash.
Depletion and amortization are the matching ideas for natural resources such as oil and for intangible assets.
An unexpected fall in an asset's value is recorded as an impairment charge.

definition.text: The ways of calculating depreciation, based either on the passage of time or on how much an asset is used.

facts.text: Straight-line depreciation, the simplest and most common, divides cost minus salvage value by the years of useful life.
Declining-balance and sum-of-years-digits methods write off more in early years, assuming assets are most productive when new.
Units-of-production depreciation charges more in years of heavy use; an asset costing $70,000 with $10,000 salvage value expected to make 6,000 units depreciates $10 per unit.

definition.text: The gradual loss in economic value of the capital stock of a firm or nation through physical wear, obsolescence or falling demand for what the capital provides.

facts.text: Next period's capital stock equals this period's stock plus gross investment minus depreciation.
Gross investment minus depreciation is net investment, the net addition to the capital stock.
Economic depreciation is the fall in the present value of the services an asset will provide in future.
An asset's value can rise instead, for example if the price of its services rises unexpectedly or the discount rate falls.
In national accounts it is called consumption of fixed capital, equal to the gap between gross and net fixed capital formation.
In the Solow–Swan growth model, a steady state occurs when gross investment equals depreciation.
